subject: biology

items.q: Which statement correctly describes how an enzyme acts as a catalyst in a cell?
items.correct: It increases the rate of a reaction that could occur without it, and is released unchanged.
items.misconception: It is converted into product along with the substrate, so the cell must keep making it.
items.why: Students learn that enzymes take part in the reaction and see the enzyme written into word equations alongside the substrate, so they treat it as one of the reactants. The idea that something can participate without being changed is unfamiliar. A catalyst increases the rate of a reaction without being used up or permanently altered. The enzyme-substrate complex releases the product and the enzyme is unchanged, so one enzyme molecule can catalyse the same reaction many thousands of times.
items.specStatementText: Enzymes speed up reactions without being used up
items.random_wrong: It makes possible a reaction that could not take place at all in its absence in the cell.

items.q: Catalase in liver cells increases the rate at which hydrogen peroxide breaks down into water and oxygen by a factor of many millions. What is the benefit to the cell of this increase in rate?
items.correct: Toxic hydrogen peroxide is removed fast enough at cell temperature to prevent damage.
items.misconception: Hydrogen peroxide could not be broken down at all without an enzyme to make it possible.
items.why: At GCSE and MYP enzymes are described as 'needed' for digestion and other reactions, and students never see the uncatalysed reaction, so they assume it does not exist rather than that it is extremely slow. Enzymes are catalysts: they increase the rate of reactions that could occur without them. The benefit to the cell is that reactions which would take years at cell temperature are completed in fractions of a second, fast enough to sustain life.
items.specStatementText: Enzymes speed up reactions without being used up
items.random_wrong: Catalase supplies the energy that the breakdown of hydrogen peroxide needs.

items.q: Which statement best describes metabolism in a living organism?
items.correct: A network of interdependent enzyme-catalysed reactions, each controlled through its own enzyme.
items.misconception: The set of reactions that release energy from food molecules to keep the organism alive and active.
items.why: In everyday use 'metabolism' means how fast a person burns calories, and the word 'metabolic rate' is linked to energy use, so students narrow the term to respiration and energy release. Metabolism is the whole network of chemical reactions in an organism. It includes anabolic reactions such as protein synthesis, glycogen formation and photosynthesis as well as catabolic reactions such as digestion and cell respiration.
items.specStatementText: Metabolism is a network of reactions, each with its own enzyme
items.random_wrong: A series of reactions whose rate is set only by how much substrate the organism takes in from outside.

items.q: A yeast cell synthesizes one amino acid through a pathway of several steps. Why does this pathway require several different enzymes rather than one?
items.correct: Each step has a different substrate, and an active site fits only one substrate.
items.misconception: One enzyme could catalyse every step if the substrates were supplied in the correct order.
items.why: At GCSE students meet only three or four digestive enzymes that seem to 'digest food' in general, and everyday talk of 'enzymes in washing powder' suggests an all-purpose chemical. Enzyme specificity means that each enzyme's active site is complementary to one substrate or one type of substrate. Because of this, many different enzymes are required by living organisms, and this is also what allows metabolism to be controlled enzyme by enzyme.
items.specStatementText: Metabolism is a network of reactions, each with its own enzyme
items.random_wrong: Each step needs a different amount of energy, and each enzyme supplies a fixed amount of energy.

items.q: Which process is an example of anabolism?
items.correct: The formation of glycogen from glucose monomers by condensation reactions
items.misconception: The oxidation of glucose in cell respiration to provide ATP for the cell
items.why: Students focus on the useful product of respiration, ATP, and apply the rule 'anabolism builds' to that product rather than to what happens to the substrate. Anabolism and catabolism are defined by what happens to the substrate. In respiration glucose is oxidized to smaller molecules, so respiration is catabolic; the energy released is used to make ATP, but that does not make the pathway anabolic.
items.specStatementText: Anabolism builds and uses energy; catabolism breaks down and releases it
items.random_wrong: The digestion of starch in the gut into maltose and then glucose

items.q: In the small intestine, maltase converts each maltose molecule into two glucose molecules. How is this reaction classified?
items.correct: Catabolic; a hydrolysis reaction in which a water molecule is used to break the glycosidic bond
items.misconception: Anabolic; the glucose produced is a useful new molecule that the body can then absorb and make use of
items.why: Everyday language says food is 'turned into nutrients', which sounds like making something, and students associate 'useful product' with building rather than breaking. Digestion is the hydrolysis of macromolecules into monomers and is an example of catabolism. The monomers are smaller than the substrate; that they are useful does not make the reaction anabolic.
items.specStatementText: Anabolism builds and uses energy; catabolism breaks down and releases it
items.random_wrong: Catabolic; a condensation reaction in which a water molecule is released as the bond is broken

items.q: A mutation replaces one amino acid in an enzyme at a position on the surface far from the active site in the folded protein. The enzyme loses most of its activity. What is the best explanation?
items.correct: The change disturbs interactions that hold the enzyme's overall shape, altering the active site
items.misconception: The result must be an error, because only the amino acids of the active site itself can affect catalysis
items.why: Diagrams show the active site as a notch on a blob, and explanations of catalysis mention only the active site, so students see the remainder of the enzyme as inert. The active site is composed of a few amino acids only, but interactions between amino acids within the overall three-dimensional structure of the enzyme ensure that the active site has the necessary properties for catalysis. Changing an amino acid elsewhere can shift these interactions and distort the active site.
items.specStatementText: The active site is a few amino acids held in place by the whole fold
items.random_wrong: The loss of activity shows the enzyme has been denatured, so its chain has broken up into free amino acids

items.q: According to the induced-fit model, what happens when a substrate binds to the active site of an enzyme?
items.correct: Both the enzyme and the substrate change shape as they bind.
items.misconception: The rigid active site admits only an exactly matching substrate.
items.why: The lock-and-key model taught at GCSE and MYP is memorable and is reinforced by rigid jigsaw-piece diagrams, so students carry it into IB unchanged. Induced fit replaces the rigid lock-and-key idea: the active site changes shape as the substrate binds, and the substrate changes shape too. This closer fit strains bonds within the substrate and is part of how the enzyme catalyses the reaction.
items.specStatementText: Enzyme and substrate both change shape as they bind
items.random_wrong: The active site closes around a substrate that keeps its shape.

items.q: ATP synthase is embedded in the inner mitochondrial membrane and cannot move freely. How do its substrates, ADP and phosphate, reach its active site?
items.correct: They move by random molecular motion in the fluid and collide with the fixed active site.
items.misconception: They cannot, so an enzyme fixed in a membrane works only after being released from it.
items.why: Students learn that molecular motion is needed for collisions and conclude that both partners must move, so a fixed enzyme seems unable to function. Movement of either partner is sufficient for collisions. Enzymes are often immobilized by being embedded in membranes and still catalyse reactions, and sometimes it is a very large substrate that is effectively immobile while the enzyme moves.
items.specStatementText: Random motion brings substrate and active site together
items.random_wrong: The enzyme extends its active site out into the fluid to capture passing substrates.

items.q: Lipase catalyses the hydrolysis of triglycerides but has no effect on starch. What is the reason?
items.correct: The active site of lipase is complementary in shape and chemical properties to a triglyceride only.
items.misconception: Starch molecules are too large to enter the active site, but any molecule smaller than starch could.
items.why: The lock-and-key picture is remembered as a matter of whether the key fits the hole, and chemical properties such as charge are invisible in the diagram. Enzyme-substrate specificity depends on the active site being complementary in both shape and chemical properties (charge, polarity) to the substrate. A molecule of the right size but the wrong shape or chemistry does not bind productively.
items.specStatementText: Active site shape explains specificity and why denaturation stops activity
items.random_wrong: Starch requires more energy to break down than lipase is able to supply to the reaction.

items.q: What happens to an enzyme when it is denatured?
items.correct: Its three-dimensional structure changes, so the active site no longer fits the substrate.
items.misconception: Its peptide bonds are broken, so the polypeptide chain splits into its separate amino acids.
items.why: Students learn that heat and acid 'destroy' enzymes and picture destruction as the molecule falling apart, confusing denaturation with hydrolysis. Denaturation is a change in the three-dimensional structure of a protein caused by breaking hydrogen bonds, ionic bonds and other interactions between amino acids. The primary structure is unchanged; the active site simply loses its shape.
items.specStatementText: Active site shape explains specificity and why denaturation stops activity
items.random_wrong: Its shape alters only briefly and then returns to normal once the conditions are restored.

items.q: A student measured the rate of an enzyme-catalysed reaction at six temperatures. The rates, in arbitrary units, were: 10 °C, 2; 20 °C, 4; 30 °C, 8; 40 °C, 15; 50 °C, 9; 60 °C, 1. Which conclusion is supported by these data?
items.correct: The optimum is near 40 °C; above it, denaturation outweighs the faster collisions.
items.misconception: The low rate at 10 °C shows that the enzyme had been denatured by the cold temperature.
items.why: Students learn that 'extremes' of temperature denature enzymes and treat the low end of the graph symmetrically with the high end. At low temperatures the rate is low because of reduced kinetic energy and fewer substrate-active site collisions, not because of denaturation. Denaturation occurs at temperatures above the optimum.
items.specStatementText: Temperature, pH and substrate concentration change the rate
items.random_wrong: The true optimum is 37 °C, the body temperature at which every enzyme works at its best.

items.q: At high substrate concentrations, the rate of an enzyme-catalysed reaction levels off even when more substrate is added. Why?
items.correct: Every active site is occupied almost all the time, so extra substrate finds no free site to bind.
items.misconception: The high concentration of substrate denatures the enzyme, so its active site stops working.
items.why: Students learn that temperature and pH beyond a limit cause denaturation and assume that substrate concentration has a similar limit. Substrate concentration does not alter the enzyme's structure. The plateau on the rate-substrate graph is caused by saturation of active sites, not by denaturation.
items.specStatementText: Temperature, pH and substrate concentration change the rate
items.random_wrong: The enzyme molecules have been used up by the reaction, so no more product can be formed.

items.q: Pepsin has an optimum pH of about 2. When it passes with food into the small intestine, where the pH is about 8, its activity falls almost to zero. Which explanation is correct?
items.correct: The change in pH alters charges on amino acids, disrupting bonds that hold the active site's shape.
items.misconception: Pepsin has run out of substrate, because protein digestion is completed inside the stomach.
items.why: Students confuse the plateau of a rate-against-concentration (or rate-against-temperature) graph, where each point is a separate run and the rate is measured at the start before any substrate has been depleted, with the flattening of a product-against-time graph, where the substrate really has run out. Each point on a rate-concentration graph is an initial rate measured before the substrate has been depleted, so the substrate cannot have run out. The plateau occurs because every active site is saturated with substrate, so the enzyme cannot work any faster.
items.specStatementText: Temperature, pH and substrate concentration change the rate
items.random_wrong: The alkaline conditions hydrolyse the peptide bonds of pepsin, breaking it up into free amino acids.

items.q: A textbook sketch graph shows the rate of an enzyme-catalysed reaction rising steadily with temperature to a sharp peak and then falling steeply. A class measured catalase activity every 5 °C from 5 °C to 70 °C and found a broad plateau between 30 °C and 45 °C rather than a sharp peak. How should the sketch graph be regarded?
items.correct: As a model of the general relationship, which the class data can be used to evaluate and refine.
items.misconception: As an accurate record of catalase results, which shows that the class must have made an error somewhere.
items.why: Sketch graphs appear in textbooks alongside real graphs and are drawn with the same confidence, so students do not distinguish a model from data. Generalized sketches of relationships are examples of models in biology. They summarize a general pattern and are evaluated, and if necessary refined, using results from enzyme experiments.
items.specStatementText: Temperature, pH and substrate concentration change the rate
items.random_wrong: As a model that the mismatch has proved to be wrong, so it should be discarded and not used again.

items.q: Catalase was added to hydrogen peroxide and the volume of oxygen collected was recorded: 0 s, 0 cm³; 20 s, 12 cm³; 40 s, 20 cm³; 60 s, 24 cm³. What is the initial rate of reaction?
items.correct: 0.6 cm³ s⁻¹
items.misconception: 0.40 cm³ s⁻¹
items.why: The everyday question is 'how much was made?', and students record the final reading and forget to divide by time, or divide the final amount by the whole time even though the reaction had already slowed. Rate is a change per unit time. The initial rate, taken from the first steep part of the graph, is the best measure; it can also be found from the time taken for a fixed event, since rate is proportional to 1/time.
items.specStatementText: Rate is change in product or substrate per unit time
items.random_wrong: 1.7 s per cm³

items.q: A filter-paper disc soaked in catalase solution sinks in hydrogen peroxide and rises when enough oxygen has formed on it. In 1% hydrogen peroxide the disc took 50 s to rise; in 2% it took 20 s. Which statement about the reaction rate is correct?
items.correct: Rate is proportional to 1/time, so the rate at 2% (0.05 s⁻¹) is 2.5 times the rate at 1% (0.02 s⁻¹).
items.misconception: The rate at 1% is 50 and at 2% is 20, so the rate fell when the concentration was doubled.
items.why: Time is the quantity actually measured with the stopwatch, and students report it as the result without converting it to a rate. A longer time means a slower reaction. To compare rates from timed experiments, calculate 1/time (or the fixed change divided by the time), so that a larger value means a faster reaction.
items.specStatementText: Rate is change in product or substrate per unit time
items.random_wrong: Doubling the concentration doubles the rate, so the rate at 2% is 0.04 s⁻¹, twice that at 1%.

items.q: How does an enzyme affect the energy changes of the reaction it catalyses?
items.correct: It lowers the activation energy but leaves the energy difference between substrate and products unchanged.
items.misconception: It lowers the energy of the products, so that more energy is released overall than would be without the enzyme.
items.why: On the energy graph the enzyme's curve is lower, and students read 'lower curve' as lower energy throughout, including the products. The catalysed curve is lower only at the peak: the enzyme lowers the activation energy. Substrate and products are at the same energy levels with or without the enzyme, so the energy yield is the same.
items.specStatementText: Enzymes lower activation energy but not the energy released
items.random_wrong: It supplies the activation energy, transferring its own energy to the substrate to break the bonds.

items.q: In an energy diagram for a reaction, the substrate is at 40 kJ mol⁻¹ and the products are at 15 kJ mol⁻¹. The highest energy reached during the reaction is 90 kJ mol⁻¹ without an enzyme and 60 kJ mol⁻¹ with the enzyme. For the enzyme-catalysed reaction, what are the activation energy and the overall energy yield?
items.correct: activation energy 20 kJ mol⁻¹; energy yield 25 kJ mol⁻¹
items.misconception: activation energy 60 kJ mol⁻¹; energy yield 25 kJ mol⁻¹
items.why: Students read the peak as a single value in the same way as they read a maximum from any other graph, forgetting that the substrate does not start at zero energy. Activation energy is the extra energy the substrate must gain to react: peak energy minus substrate energy. With an enzyme the peak is lower, so this difference is smaller.
items.specStatementText: Enzymes lower activation energy but not the energy released
items.random_wrong: activation energy 20 kJ mol⁻¹; energy yield 45 kJ mol⁻¹

items.q: Which statement about intracellular and extracellular enzyme-catalysed reactions is correct?
items.correct: Glycolysis is intracellular; chemical digestion in the gut is extracellular.
items.misconception: Digestion in the gut is intracellular, because food is broken down inside the cells that line it.
items.why: Students know cells absorb the products of digestion and that enzymes are made in cells, and they merge the two into a picture of food being taken into cells and digested there. Digestive enzymes are synthesized in cells and secreted into the gut lumen, where they hydrolyse food macromolecules. Chemical digestion in the gut is the standard example of an extracellular enzyme-catalysed reaction.
items.specStatementText: Enzymes act inside cells or are secreted to act outside
items.random_wrong: The Krebs cycle is extracellular, because it breaks down food in the gut to release its energy.

items.q: A resting mammal produces heat continuously, even when it is not shivering and its muscles are relaxed. Why is this heat production inevitable?
items.correct: No metabolic reaction transfers energy with 100% efficiency, so part of the energy of every reaction becomes heat.
items.misconception: Heat is produced only by dedicated reactions, such as those in shivering muscle, which are switched on when cold.
items.why: Respiration is taught as 'releasing energy for ATP', and shivering and brown fat are taught as the ways mammals make heat, so heat seems to come only from dedicated mechanisms. Heat generation is inevitable because metabolic reactions are not 100% efficient in energy transfer. Every reaction of metabolism, in every organism, releases some heat; shivering only adds to this background production.
items.specStatementText: Metabolism always makes heat, and some animals depend on it
items.random_wrong: Breaking the bonds in glucose releases energy directly as heat before any of it is transferred to make ATP.

items.q: What distinguishes the Calvin cycle and the Krebs cycle from glycolysis?
items.correct: In the cycles an intermediate used in the first step is regenerated in the last, whereas glycolysis runs from glucose to pyruvate in a chain.
items.misconception: The cycles regenerate all of their intermediates and so produce no net product, whereas glycolysis produces pyruvate as its end product.
items.why: The circular diagram has no obvious beginning or end, and the arrows entering and leaving are easy to overlook. In a cyclical pathway the product of the last reaction is the substrate of the first, so that intermediate is regenerated. Other substrates enter and net products leave: the Krebs cycle releases carbon dioxide and reduced NAD, and the Calvin cycle releases triose phosphate.
items.specStatementText: Pathways run as a line or as a cycle
items.random_wrong: The cycles use up their starting compound on every turn, so it must be supplied continuously from outside, unlike the glucose used in glycolysis.

items.q: Which statement about non-competitive inhibition at an allosteric site is correct?
items.correct: The inhibitor binds reversibly away from the active site, and the resulting shape change stops catalysis.
items.misconception: The inhibitor binds permanently to the allosteric site, so the enzyme is inactivated for the rest of its life.
items.why: The word 'non-competitive' is read as meaning the inhibitor 'cannot be removed', and students conflate non-competitive inhibition with irreversible inhibition. Binding to an allosteric site is reversible. Non-competitive inhibition differs from competitive inhibition in where the inhibitor binds and in the effect of substrate concentration, not in being permanent; irreversible inhibition is a separate category.
items.specStatementText: Binding at an allosteric site reshapes the active site
items.random_wrong: Any molecule of a suitable size can occupy the allosteric site, and it denatures the enzyme when it does so.

items.q: The rate of an enzyme-catalysed reaction was measured at six increasing substrate concentrations, without and with inhibitor X. Without X the rates were 20, 35, 50, 58, 60 and 60 units. With X they were 8, 18, 33, 48, 57 and 60 units. What type of inhibitor is X?
items.correct: Competitive, because at high substrate concentration the inhibited rate reaches the uninhibited maximum.
items.misconception: Non-competitive, because a competitive inhibitor would have kept the rate low at every substrate concentration.
items.why: Diagrams show the inhibitor 'plugging' the active site, and the everyday sense of 'block' is a fixed obstruction. Competitive inhibition is a consequence of an inhibitor binding reversibly to an active site. Substrate and inhibitor compete for the site, so raising the substrate concentration reduces the fraction of time the inhibitor is bound.
items.specStatementText: Competitive inhibitors share the active site with the substrate
items.random_wrong: Non-competitive, because X lowers the rate at most concentrations, which shows that it is bound irreversibly.

items.q: Statins are drugs prescribed to reduce blood cholesterol. How do they act?
items.correct: They resemble the substrate of an enzyme in the cholesterol synthesis pathway and bind reversibly to its active site.
items.misconception: They hydrolyse cholesterol molecules that are already circulating in the blood into products that are excreted.
items.why: Statins are advertised as 'lowering cholesterol', and the most obvious way to lower something is to remove it. Statins resemble the substrate of HMG-CoA reductase and bind reversibly to its active site. They reduce the rate of cholesterol synthesis; they do not digest cholesterol.
items.specStatementText: Competitive inhibitors share the active site with the substrate
items.random_wrong: They bind permanently to the active site of the enzyme, so cholesterol synthesis stops for the rest of life.

items.q: In bacteria, threonine is converted into isoleucine by a pathway of five enzyme-catalysed steps. What happens when isoleucine is added to a growing culture?
items.correct: Isoleucine binds to an allosteric site on the first enzyme, reversibly reducing the pathway's activity.
items.misconception: Isoleucine binds to the enzyme of the final step, the one that produced it, and blocks that single step only.
items.why: Proximity seems logical: the product is next to the last enzyme on the diagram, so that is the enzyme it is imagined to affect. In feedback inhibition the end product acts as an inhibitor of the first enzyme in the pathway. Isoleucine inhibits threonine deaminase, the first enzyme of the pathway from threonine, which stops the whole pathway and prevents wasteful build-up of intermediates.
items.specStatementText: The end product switches off the first enzyme
items.random_wrong: The five enzymes are broken down, so the pathway cannot restart after the isoleucine is used up.

items.q: Penicillin inhibits transpeptidases, the bacterial enzymes that cross-link peptidoglycan in the cell wall. Which statement correctly describes both the action of penicillin and how bacteria become resistant to it?
items.correct: Penicillin bonds irreversibly to the active site, changing it chemically; a changed transpeptidase that penicillin cannot bind confers resistance.
items.misconception: Penicillin competes reversibly with the substrate for the active site; bacteria resist it by producing extra substrate that outcompetes the drug molecules.
items.why: Students learn that active-site inhibitors are competitive and reversible, and penicillin binds at the active site. Mechanism-based inhibition is a consequence of chemical changes to the active site caused by the irreversible binding of an inhibitor. Penicillin bonds covalently to transpeptidase, so cross-linking of peptidoglycan stops and the bacterium is unable to maintain its cell wall.
items.specStatementText: Some inhibitors change the active site for good
items.random_wrong: Penicillin binds to an allosteric site on transpeptidase and inactivates it permanently; resistant bacteria have a transpeptidase that lacks the allosteric site.

items.q: Where does the energy come from for a substrate to react when an enzyme is present?
items.correct: From the substrate molecules' own kinetic energy; the enzyme lowers the activation energy so that more of the molecules already have enough energy to react. The enzyme does not supply energy.
items.misconception: An enzyme supplies or transfers energy to the substrate to make the reaction go.
items.why: Enzymes are described as 'helping' reactions and as being 'active', and students know that reactions need activation energy, so the natural conclusion is that the enzyme provides it. Enzymes lower the activation energy of a reaction by binding the substrate so that bonds within it are strained and easier to break. No energy is supplied by the enzyme; the energy comes from the reacting molecules themselves.
items.specStatementText: Enzymes speed up reactions without being used up
items.note: an MCQ carries this misconception as a secondary distractor only (one item per stem); its own authored question is used here, and no third distractor was authored for it; none invented

items.q: How does a cell control the rate of a metabolic pathway?
items.correct: Chiefly by controlling its enzymes: how much of each enzyme is made and whether each enzyme molecule is active, for example through inhibitors.
items.misconception: The rate of metabolism is set only by how much substrate the organism takes in; enzymes are permanently active and cannot be regulated.
items.why: Students first meet rate as something that depends on substrate concentration and temperature, and the enzyme is pictured as a fixed piece of machinery, so it is not seen as something the cell can switch on or off. Because each reaction of metabolism depends on its own specific enzyme, control over metabolism can be exerted through these enzymes. Cells regulate enzyme synthesis and enzyme activity, so that the rate of a pathway is not simply a consequence of how much substrate is available.
items.specStatementText: Metabolism is a network of reactions, each with its own enzyme
items.note: an MCQ carries this misconception as a secondary distractor only (one item per stem); its own authored question is used here, and no third distractor was authored for it; none invented

items.q: Do catabolic reactions need an input of energy?
items.correct: No. Catabolic reactions, such as hydrolysis in digestion and oxidation in respiration, release energy; it is anabolic reactions that require energy.
items.misconception: Catabolic reactions need an input of energy to break the molecule apart, and anabolic reactions release energy as the new molecule is put together.
items.why: In everyday experience breaking things takes effort, and students have also learned that energy is required to break bonds, which they over-generalize to the whole reaction rather than to its first step. Although energy is needed to break bonds within the substrate, more energy is released when the bonds of the products form, so catabolic reactions such as hydrolysis and oxidation release energy overall. Anabolic reactions, which form macromolecules from monomers by condensation, require an input of energy.
items.specStatementText: Anabolism builds and uses energy; catabolism breaks down and releases it
items.note: an MCQ carries this misconception as a secondary distractor only (one item per stem); its own authored question is used here, and no third distractor was authored for it; none invented

items.q: Is water used or released when a bond between two monomers is broken?
items.correct: Water is used: hydrolysis adds a water molecule to break the bond. Water is released in condensation, when monomers are joined.
items.misconception: Water is released when a bond between monomers is broken, and water is used up when monomers are joined.
items.why: The everyday meaning of condensation is water appearing on a cold surface, and 'hydrolysis' is misread as 'splitting off water', so students attach water release to the wrong reaction. Condensation joins monomers by forming a covalent bond and releasing a water molecule; hydrolysis breaks the bond by adding a water molecule. Formation of macromolecules is by condensation and their digestion is by hydrolysis.
items.specStatementText: Anabolism builds and uses energy; catabolism breaks down and releases it
items.note: an MCQ carries this misconception as a secondary distractor only (one item per stem); its own authored question is used here, and no third distractor was authored for it; none invented

items.q: Which molecule changes shape during induced-fit binding?
items.correct: Both the enzyme and the substrate change shape when binding occurs.
items.misconception: Only the enzyme changes shape in induced fit; the substrate is a fixed shape that the active site moulds itself around.
items.why: The name 'induced fit' and most animations emphasize the active site closing around the substrate, so the change in the substrate goes unnoticed. Students should recognize that both substrate and enzyme change shape when binding occurs. The change in the substrate weakens bonds within it and is part of the mechanism of catalysis.
items.specStatementText: Enzyme and substrate both change shape as they bind
items.note: an MCQ carries this misconception as a secondary distractor only (one item per stem); its own authored question is used here, and no third distractor was authored for it; none invented

items.q: What makes molecules in the cytoplasm move?
items.correct: Nothing has to make them move: molecules in a fluid are in continuous random motion because of their kinetic energy.
items.misconception: Molecules in a cell are stationary until something pushes or carries them, so substrates must be transported to an enzyme.
items.why: Everyday objects stay still unless moved, and students have not internalized that at the molecular scale particles are in constant random motion. Substrates and enzymes move by random molecular motion, which is what brings a substrate and an active site together. Raising the temperature increases this motion and so increases the frequency of collisions.
items.specStatementText: Random motion brings substrate and active site together
items.note: an MCQ carries this misconception as a secondary distractor only (one item per stem); its own authored question is used here, and no third distractor was authored for it; none invented

items.q: If an enzyme is denatured by heat, does its activity return when it is cooled?
items.correct: Usually not. Heat denaturation is generally permanent, because the polypeptide does not refold correctly once its shape has been lost.
items.misconception: Denaturation is a temporary change; cooling the enzyme allows it to refold and recover its full activity.
items.why: Reducing the temperature below the optimum lowers activity in a way that is reversible, and students extend that reversibility to the loss of activity above the optimum. Below the optimum, changes in rate are reversible because the enzyme's shape is unchanged. Above the optimum the enzyme is denatured: its three-dimensional structure is disrupted and the active site is lost, and this is normally irreversible.
items.specStatementText: Active site shape explains specificity and why denaturation stops activity
items.note: an MCQ carries this misconception as a secondary distractor only (one item per stem); its own authored question is used here, and no third distractor was authored for it; none invented

items.q: Are enzymes living things that can be killed?
items.correct: No. Enzymes are protein molecules; heat or extreme pH denatures them, changing their shape, but they are not alive.
items.misconception: Enzymes are tiny living things, so heat or acid kills them.
items.why: Everyday and even classroom language speaks of enzymes being 'killed' by boiling, and the word 'active' suggests something alive. Enzymes are globular proteins. Denaturation is a change in the three-dimensional structure of the molecule that destroys the active site; it is a chemical change to a molecule, not the death of an organism.
items.specStatementText: Active site shape explains specificity and why denaturation stops activity
items.note: an MCQ carries this misconception as a secondary distractor only (one item per stem); its own authored question is used here, and no third distractor was authored for it; none invented

items.q: Do all enzymes have an optimum of 37 °C and pH 7?
items.correct: No. Optima differ between enzymes: pepsin's optimum pH is about 2, and enzymes from thermophilic bacteria have optimum temperatures well above 37 °C.
items.misconception: Every enzyme works best at 37 °C and pH 7, because those are the conditions of the human body.
items.why: Human enzymes dominate the examples taught, and the sketch graphs used in class usually have their peak drawn at body temperature and neutral pH. Each enzyme has its own optimum temperature and optimum pH, adapted to where it works. The sketch graph shows the general shape of the relationship, not fixed values for every enzyme.
items.specStatementText: Temperature, pH and substrate concentration change the rate
items.note: an MCQ carries this misconception as a secondary distractor only (one item per stem); its own authored question is used here, and no third distractor was authored for it; none invented

items.q: Does the rate keep rising in proportion to substrate concentration?
items.correct: No. Rate rises with substrate concentration at first but levels off at a maximum when all active sites are saturated.
items.misconception: The rate of an enzyme-catalysed reaction is proportional to the substrate concentration at every concentration, so doubling the substrate doubles the rate.
items.why: The first part of the rate-substrate graph is close to a straight line, and students extend the proportional relationship they see there to the whole graph. At low substrate concentration rate rises as collisions become more frequent, but as active sites become saturated the increase slows and the rate reaches a plateau. Beyond this, adding substrate does not increase the rate.
items.specStatementText: Temperature, pH and substrate concentration change the rate
items.note: an MCQ carries this misconception as a secondary distractor only (one item per stem); its own authored question is used here, and no third distractor was authored for it; none invented

items.q: How does a change in pH reduce the rate of an enzyme-catalysed reaction?
items.correct: By changing the charges on amino acids in the enzyme, which disrupts ionic and hydrogen bonds and alters the shape of the active site.
items.misconception: A change in pH slows the reaction because the molecules move more slowly and collide less often.
items.why: Collision theory is used to explain the effect of temperature and substrate concentration, and students apply the same explanation to pH without noticing that pH does not change molecular speed. pH affects rate through the enzyme's structure. Hydrogen ions alter the charges on amino acids, disrupting the bonds that hold the active site in shape; at extreme pH the enzyme is denatured. Collision frequency is not the mechanism.
items.specStatementText: Temperature, pH and substrate concentration change the rate
items.note: an MCQ carries this misconception as a secondary distractor only (one item per stem); its own authored question is used here, and no third distractor was authored for it; none invented

items.q: If experimental results do not match a model exactly, should the model be discarded?
items.correct: Not necessarily. A model is a simplification; a mismatch is evaluated and may lead to the model being refined, or to the limits of its usefulness being recognized.
items.misconception: A model is either right or wrong, so any mismatch with data proves it wrong and it must be abandoned.
items.why: School science is often presented as facts that are true or false, so the idea of a deliberately simplified representation with limits is unfamiliar. Models in the form of sketch graphs are evaluated using results from enzyme experiments. Evaluation can confirm the general pattern, identify where the model is too simple, or lead to a refined model; it does not mean discarding any model that is imperfect.
items.specStatementText: Temperature, pH and substrate concentration change the rate
items.note: an MCQ carries this misconception as a secondary distractor only (one item per stem); its own authored question is used here, and no third distractor was authored for it; none invented

items.q: Is energy released when bonds in the substrate are broken?
items.correct: No. Energy is required to break bonds; energy is released when the bonds of the products are formed.
items.misconception: Breaking bonds releases energy, which is where the energy of a reaction comes from.
items.why: ATP is described as having 'high-energy bonds' that release energy when broken, and students generalize this shorthand to all bonds. Energy is required to break bonds within the substrate, and this is why a reaction needs activation energy. There is an energy yield when bonds are made to form the products; the reaction releases energy overall when more is released in bond making than was needed for bond breaking.
items.specStatementText: Enzymes lower activation energy but not the energy released
items.note: an MCQ carries this misconception as a secondary distractor only (one item per stem); its own authored question is used here, and no third distractor was authored for it; none invented

items.q: On an energy graph, how is the energy released by the reaction read?
items.correct: As the difference between the energy of the substrate and the energy of the products.
items.misconception: The energy released is the fall from the top of the peak down to the products.
items.why: The steep drop after the peak is the most striking feature of the graph, and it looks like the energy 'coming out' of the reaction. The energy yield of an exothermic reaction is the substrate energy minus the product energy. The fall from the peak includes the activation energy that was put in, which is returned rather than released.
items.specStatementText: Enzymes lower activation energy but not the energy released
items.note: an MCQ carries this misconception as a secondary distractor only (one item per stem); its own authored question is used here, and no third distractor was authored for it; none invented

items.q: Where are extracellular enzymes made?
items.correct: Inside cells, by ribosomes; they are then secreted and act outside the cell.
items.misconception: Extracellular enzymes are made outside cells, which is why they act there.
items.why: The prefix 'extra-' is read as describing where the enzyme comes from rather than where it acts. All enzymes are proteins synthesized inside cells. An extracellular enzyme is one that is secreted and catalyses its reaction outside cells, such as the digestive enzymes in the gut.
items.specStatementText: Enzymes act inside cells or are secreted to act outside
items.note: an MCQ carries this misconception as a secondary distractor only (one item per stem); its own authored question is used here, and no third distractor was authored for it; none invented

items.q: Is cell respiration a form of digestion?
items.correct: No. Digestion is the extracellular hydrolysis of food in the gut; respiration is the intracellular oxidation of substrates such as glucose, through glycolysis and the Krebs cycle.
items.misconception: The Krebs cycle and the other reactions of respiration take place in the gut, breaking down food to release energy.
items.why: Both processes are described as 'breaking down food to get energy', so students merge them into one process located in the digestive system. Glycolysis and the Krebs cycle are intracellular: glycolysis occurs in the cytoplasm and the Krebs cycle in mitochondria of every respiring cell. Chemical digestion in the gut is extracellular and produces the monomers that cells later respire.
items.specStatementText: Enzymes act inside cells or are secreted to act outside
items.note: an MCQ carries this misconception as a secondary distractor only (one item per stem); its own authored question is used here, and no third distractor was authored for it; none invented

items.q: Do animals other than mammals and birds produce metabolic heat?
items.correct: Yes. All organisms produce heat from metabolism; mammals, birds and some other animals differ in depending on it to maintain a constant body temperature.
items.misconception: Only warm-blooded animals produce heat; the reactions in cold-blooded animals transfer their energy without any loss as heat.
items.why: The labels 'warm-blooded' and 'cold-blooded' suggest that heat production itself is what differs between the groups. Metabolic reactions in every organism release heat because energy transfer is never 100% efficient. What distinguishes mammals and birds is that they rely on this heat production to maintain a constant body temperature.
items.specStatementText: Metabolism always makes heat, and some animals depend on it
items.note: an MCQ carries this misconception as a secondary distractor only (one item per stem); its own authored question is used here, and no third distractor was authored for it; none invented

items.q: Is the starting compound of a cycle used up and in need of continual resupply?
items.correct: No. It is regenerated by the last reaction of the cycle; only the other inputs need to be supplied.
items.misconception: The starting compound of a cycle is consumed each turn, so the cell must keep supplying it from outside.
items.why: In a linear pathway the starting substrate is consumed, and students apply the same logic to the first compound they see on a cycle diagram. The defining feature of a cyclical pathway is that the intermediate consumed in the first step is regenerated in the last: RuBP in the Calvin cycle and oxaloacetate in the Krebs cycle. What must be supplied continuously is the other substrate that enters each turn.
items.specStatementText: Pathways run as a line or as a cycle
items.note: an MCQ carries this misconception as a secondary distractor only (one item per stem); its own authored question is used here, and no third distractor was authored for it; none invented

items.q: Is non-competitive inhibition the same as denaturation?
items.correct: No. A specific molecule binds reversibly to an allosteric site and causes a conformational change that alters the active site; the enzyme is not denatured and recovers when the inhibitor leaves.
items.misconception: A non-competitive inhibitor is any molecule that can bind to the enzyme and denature it by changing its shape.
items.why: Both denaturation and non-competitive inhibition are explained as 'changing the shape of the active site', so the two are merged. Only specific substances can bind to an allosteric site. Binding causes interactions within the enzyme that lead to conformational changes, which alter the active site enough to prevent catalysis, but the change is reversible and the enzyme's structure is not destroyed.
items.specStatementText: Binding at an allosteric site reshapes the active site
items.note: an MCQ carries this misconception as a secondary distractor only (one item per stem); its own authored question is used here, and no third distractor was authored for it; none invented

items.q: Does increasing the substrate concentration overcome non-competitive inhibition?
items.correct: No. Because the inhibitor does not compete for the active site, extra substrate does not displace it and the maximum rate stays reduced.
items.misconception: Adding more substrate overcomes any reversible inhibitor, because the substrate outcompetes it.
items.why: The idea that 'more substrate wins' is learned for competitive inhibitors and then applied to all inhibitors. Competitive and non-competitive inhibition differ in the interactions between substrate and inhibitor and therefore in the effect of substrate concentration. Only competitive inhibition is overcome at high substrate concentration.
items.specStatementText: Competitive inhibitors share the active site with the substrate
items.note: an MCQ carries this misconception as a secondary distractor only (one item per stem); its own authored question is used here, and no third distractor was authored for it; none invented

items.q: Is feedback inhibition permanent?
items.correct: No. The end product binds reversibly to an allosteric site, so when its concentration falls the inhibition is released and the pathway resumes.
items.misconception: Feedback inhibition switches the pathway off for good; the enzymes are destroyed or their genes are permanently silenced.
items.why: Students confuse regulation of enzyme activity with regulation of gene expression, and the word 'inhibition' is taken to mean a permanent stop. Feedback inhibition is reversible non-competitive inhibition. It provides moment-to-moment control: the pathway slows when isoleucine accumulates and speeds up again as isoleucine is used in protein synthesis.
items.specStatementText: The end product switches off the first enzyme
items.note: an MCQ carries this misconception as a secondary distractor only (one item per stem); its own authored question is used here, and no third distractor was authored for it; none invented

items.q: Where on the first enzyme does the end product bind in feedback inhibition?
items.correct: At an allosteric site, away from the active site; binding changes the enzyme's conformation and so its active site.
items.misconception: The end product binds to the active site and competes with the substrate for it.
items.why: Students learn competitive inhibition first and default to the active site as the place any inhibitor binds. The end product is usually chemically unlike the substrate of the first enzyme, so it cannot compete for the active site. It binds to an allosteric site: isoleucine binds to an allosteric site on threonine deaminase, not to the site that binds threonine.
items.specStatementText: The end product switches off the first enzyme
items.note: an MCQ carries this misconception as a secondary distractor only (one item per stem); its own authored question is used here, and no third distractor was authored for it; none invented

items.q: How does a bacterial population become resistant to penicillin?
items.correct: A mutation produces a changed transpeptidase whose active site no longer binds penicillin effectively; bacteria with this enzyme survive and reproduce, so the population becomes resistant.
items.misconception: Individual bacteria exposed to penicillin alter their own transpeptidase during their lifetime and pass the change on.
items.why: Everyday phrases such as 'building up a resistance' imply that exposure causes the change, rather than selecting bacteria that already carry it. Resistance arises from a heritable change to transpeptidases: a mutant enzyme that still cross-links peptidoglycan but does not bind penicillin. Penicillin does not cause the mutation; it selects for the bacteria that already have it.
items.specStatementText: Some inhibitors change the active site for good
items.note: an MCQ carries this misconception as a secondary distractor only (one item per stem); its own authored question is used here, and no third distractor was authored for it; none invented
